items.stem: All of the following acts of President Ronald Reagan’s administration are characterized as a return to conservative political values EXCEPT
options: (B) nominating Sandra Day O'Connor to the Court
items.explanation: In 1981, Ronald Reagan, in a move supported by various groups across the political spectrum, made Sandra Day O’Connor the first woman to serve on the Supreme Court. All the other choices represent typically conservative policy decisions by Reagan.

option_explanations.A: Cutting the federal budget was a core conservative Reagan policy — not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Nominating Sandra Day O'Connor in 1981 — the first woman on the Supreme Court — was supported across the political spectrum and was not specifically a conservative ideological move, so it is the exception.
option_explanations.C: Cutting corporate taxes was a core conservative Reagan policy — not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Loosening government regulation of business was a core conservative Reagan policy — not the exception.

items.stem: Which of the following did NOT contribute to the emergence of the New Right of the 1970s and 1980s?
options: (D) A sudden drop in the stock market
items.explanation: Although there was a brief drop in the stock market in 1987 (known as Black Monday), this was not a contributing factor to the emergence of the New Right. All of the other factors did lead to this renewal of conservatism.

option_explanations.A: The Moral Majority, founded by Jerry Falwell in 1979, mobilized evangelical Christians into politics and was a driving force of the New Right — not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Ronald Reagan's popularity embodied and led the New Right's rise — not the exception.
option_explanations.C: The stagflation of the 1970s discredited liberal economic management and fueled the conservative turn — not the exception.
option_explanations.D: The sharp 1987 stock-market drop (Black Monday, October 19, 1987) came after the New Right had already emerged and elected Reagan twice. It did not contribute to the movement's rise — this is the exception.

items.stem: In the 1990s, the conservative distaste for the changing demographics of the United States fueled
options: (A) the increasing racial and ethnic diversity of the United States
(B) a series of laws mandating bilingual education
(C) laws restricting the employment of undocumented immigrants
(D) increased spending on social services and more ethnic media content
items.explanation: After 40 years of restricted immigration, in the 1960s the federal government threw open the gates to immigrants from around the world. As a result, the United States was flooded with legal immigrants from almost every conceivable nation, which caused cultural conservatives to feel that their country was losing its identity. While conservatives couldn’t restrict legal immigration, they were able to respond by restricting illegal immigration—a much more popular cause, politically. Choice (A) is a cause, not an effect, so eliminate it. Choice (B) is a reversal; bilingual education was abolished in some states, so eliminate that too. Choice (D) confuses causes; if there was more social spending or ethnic media, it certainly wasn’t because of conservative distaste for immigrants. Eliminate (D).

option_explanations.A: Increasing racial and ethnic diversity was the cause of conservative anxiety, not its effect. The question asks what the distaste fueled.
option_explanations.B: This reverses the history. Conservatives opposed bilingual education (e.g., California's Proposition 227 in 1998 abolished it); they did not mandate it.
option_explanations.C: Unable to restrict legal immigration politically, conservatives channeled their response into restricting illegal immigration — employer sanctions and measures like California's Proposition 187 (1994) targeting undocumented immigrants' access to jobs and services.
option_explanations.D: Conservatives pushed to cut social-services spending, not increase it. More spending is the opposite of their position.
